chapter_theme: Songs at Tiruvathigai (திருவதிகை) on the Kedilam river, where Siva burned the three cities: two confessions about common women and their bed, one asking to be rid of the mind's whirling, the other to escape the sea of births and the two deeds by naming Murugan's twelve arms; one praise calls Murugan the poet who received his songs at the wish of the Lady of Kailasa.

737.reading: The poet describes common women whose eyes close like carp, whose voices falter like cuckoos and parrots, who give the nectar of coral lips, whose breasts sway, whose hair slips and waists sag as their garments fall in lovemaking on the flower bed, and asks Murugan to remove the anxiety of his mind, whirling in that sweet union, before he melts away. The praise names the nephew of Achyuta, whose arrow cut the ten heads of the dark asura, the poet of honour who received his poems in full as the Lady on the left of the lord of Kailasa wished, and the lord of Tiruvathigai, where the Kedilam floods past areca and plantain and the drums beat.
737.nuance: கயிலைமலைக் கிழவன் இடக் குமரி விருப்பொடு கருதக் கவி நிறையப் பெறும் வரிசைப் புலவோனே: Murugan as the poet favoured by Uma may point to Sambandar, whom she fed with milk and who then sang, and whom the book often makes Murugan; the text does not name him. பொதுமாதர் are women common to all, but money is not mentioned.

738.reading: The poet speaks of women with eyes of poison and spears, nectar words and artful breasts, poisonous ones who cast the deeds and the lives of even manly and handsome men into their double net, and asks that he not join them or suffer, but in the company of those who think of Murugan never be lost in the sea of seven births nor sink in the baseness of the two deeds, and be given to say each day, 'Lord, your twelve arms', which freed the gods, sages and Indra from their trouble. The praise names Rama who brought down Ravana's twenty arms and ten crowned heads with one arrow and shot fire into the sea, Vishnu asleep on the serpent in the milk sea, as uncle, the peacock hero of the battle, and the lord of Devayanai at Adhigai, where the cruel demons' three cities were burned.
738.nuance: உனை நினைபவர் துணைகொள: the company of devotees is the remedy, as in 722. இருவலை, the double net, catches both deeds and life. The shrine's own myth, the burning of the three cities (திரிபுரம் எரிசெய்த அதிகை), closes the song.

links.note: Both ask to be set among the Lord's devotees as the way out of the round of births: 722 asks to be counted in the throng of servants, 738 to have those who think of Murugan as companions so as not to drown in the sea of seven births.

737 calls Murugan the poet of honour whose verses filled as the Lady on the left of Kailasa's lord wished (கயிலைமலைக் கிழவன் இடக் குமரி விருப்பொடு கருதக் கவி நிறையப் பெறும்). 542 says his mouth smells of the nectar that welled from the first Goddess's breast (பரைமுலையின் ஊறி எழும் அமிர்தம்) and names him the wise one of Kazhi. 542 makes plain the Sambandar story that 737 only touches: the poet's gift comes from the Goddess.

738 asks that, in the company of those who think of Murugan (உனை நினைபவர் துணைகொள), he not be lost in the sea of seven births (எழு பிறவியெனு உவரியினிடை கெடாது). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song keeps the sea and adds the devotees' company as the means of crossing.
